title: IS ENJOYING YOUR SPOUSE’S BODY “LUST”?
paragraphs: IS ENJOYING YOUR SPOUSE’S BODY “LUST”?
The Bible’s Answer Requires a Better Definition of Lust—and It May Heal Something Shame Has Been Breaking Inside Christian Marriages for Years
There is a husband somewhere who looks at his wife and still thinks she is breathtaking.
Then he feels guilty for thinking it.

There is a wife somewhere who deeply desires her husband, loves his touch, notices his body, longs to be close to him—and somewhere along the way she absorbed the idea that being “spiritual” means becoming almost embarrassed by those feelings.
So they love Jesus.
They love each other.
They are married.
They are faithful.
And somehow, in the very place God designed for covenant intimacy, shame has crawled into the bedroom and started whispering...
“Maybe wanting your spouse this much is lust.”
That sentence sounds holy.
But is it biblical?
Because if every strong sexual desire is automatically lust, we have a serious problem.
The Bible itself celebrates marital desire.
Not reluctantly.
Not apologetically.
Not with its eyes closed.
It celebrates it with language so surprisingly physical that some Christians become uncomfortable reading it aloud.
And perhaps that discomfort reveals something.
Maybe some of us have spent so long fighting sexual sin that we accidentally began treating sexuality itself as sinful.
Those are not the same thing.
Jesus absolutely condemns lust.
Jesus absolutely confronts adultery of the heart.
Jesus absolutely calls His followers to sexual holiness.
But before we put something under the judgment of Christ, we should make sure we understand what Christ actually condemned.
Listen carefully to Matthew 5:28 in Greek:
“πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν...”
A central word is ἐπιθυμέω—epithymeō.

It can mean to desire, long for, set one’s desire upon, or covet. The word itself is not a magical Greek synonym meaning that every experience of attraction is automatically sinful. Scripture can use this word-family for desires whose moral character depends upon their object and context.
That matters.
A lot.
Because Jesus is not teaching that the human ability to recognize beauty is adultery.
He is taking the command against adultery all the way into the heart.
Matthew 5 does not permit us to say, “I never physically committed adultery, therefore my heart is clean.”
Jesus destroys that loophole.
A person can cultivate an adulterous desire internally before committing an adulterous act externally.
Sin can begin before skin ever touches skin.
The eyes can become servants of covetousness.
The imagination can take what covenant has not given.
Another human being can become an object consumed inside the mind.
That is why Jesus’ teaching is so devastating.
He does not merely ask, “What did your body do?”
He asks what your heart is doing.
But now comes the distinction Christians desperately need.
Your spouse is not your neighbor’s spouse.
Covenant desire for your husband or wife is not identical to coveting someone outside that covenant.
In fact, Proverbs gives us language that would sound almost scandalous if we had not already been told it was Scripture.
“Rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
Then Proverbs 5:19 becomes startlingly physical:
“Let her breasts satisfy thee at all times; and be thou ravished always with her love.”
That is the King James Version.
Not a romance novel.
Not secular culture.
Proverbs.
The Hebrew behind the final image includes the verb שָׁגָה—shagah—a word capable of carrying the imagery of reeling, wandering, or being intoxicated or captivated.
Think about that.
God’s wisdom literature does not merely tolerate a husband delighting in his wife.
It tells him to be captivated by her love.
The text does not say, “Try not to notice her body.”
It specifically mentions her body.
And it places that physical delight inside marital faithfulness.
That changes the conversation completely.
The biblical opposite of sexual immorality is not necessarily sexual indifference.
It is sexual holiness.
And holiness is not the destruction of every desire.
Holiness puts desire where it belongs.
Fire in a fireplace can warm a home.
Fire consuming the curtains can destroy it.
The problem is not that fire possesses heat.
The question is where the fire is burning.
That is why Song of Songs can speak with such breathtaking freedom about physical beauty.
The lovers notice each other.
They desire each other.
They describe each other.
They long for each other.
Bodies are not treated as embarrassing accidents attached to otherwise spiritual people.
Why?
Because Christianity does not teach that the body is inherently dirty.
God created humanity embodied.
Genesis does not end the creation of male and female with God saying, “This is unfortunate but necessary.”
God looked upon His creation and called it very good.
Sin corrupted human sexuality.
Sin did not invent human sexuality.
There is an enormous difference.
And when Christians confuse those two truths, something painful happens.
A young man may spend years hearing, “Don’t look. Don’t desire. Don’t think sexually. Control yourself.”
Some of that instruction may be desperately necessary.
Pornography must be resisted.
Fornication must be resisted.
Adultery must be resisted.
Using people must be resisted.
Coveting must be resisted.
Sexual fantasy that violates covenant faithfulness must be resisted.
Then the young man gets married.
Suddenly he is supposed to understand that his wife’s body is not something dirty.
But nobody helped him distinguish sinful coveting from holy marital desire.
A Christian woman can carry another version of the same wound.
She may have been taught modesty in ways that unintentionally left her believing her body was primarily dangerous.
Something that caused men to stumble.
Something to cover.
Something about which good Christian women should remain embarrassed.
Then she marries a man who looks at her with affection and desire.
And instead of feeling cherished, part of her wonders...
“Is he being lustful?”
Sometimes, of course, there can be genuinely sinful behavior inside marriage.
Marriage is not a magic word that turns selfishness into holiness.
A wedding ring does not authorize cruelty.
Your spouse is a person to love, not an object to consume.
Biblical marital intimacy must never become justification for coercion, degradation, manipulation, humiliation, violence, betrayal, pornography, comparison with other people, or selfish entitlement.
And this is precisely where 1 Corinthians 7 becomes so important.
Paul speaks about marital intimacy with striking reciprocity.
The husband has obligations toward his wife.
The wife has obligations toward her husband.
And when Paul discusses temporary abstinence, he speaks of agreement—mutuality.
Notice how radically different this is from using another person's body.
Biblical intimacy says, in effect:
I belong to you, and you belong to me.
Not...
You exist for me.
There is tenderness in that difference.
There is covenant in that difference.
There is Christlike self-giving in that difference.
Healthy marital desire asks, “How can I love you?”
Lust distorted by sin asks, “How can I consume you?”
Love sees a person.
Sin reduces a person to a product.
Love can wait.
Sin demands.
Love honors boundaries.
Sin resents them.
Love remains faithful when circumstances change.
Objectification becomes angry when the object stops satisfying it.
Love cares about the soul attached to the body.
And this is where some marriages need more than a definition.
They need healing.
Maybe your spouse’s body has changed.
Pregnancy changed it.
Childbirth changed it.
Age changed it.
Illness changed it.
Medication changed it.
Stress changed it.
Work changed it.
Grief changed it.
Years changed it.
Your own body changed too.
The honeymoon photographs are somewhere in a drawer, and neither of you looks exactly like those two people anymore.
But covenant love was never supposed to survive only while gravity cooperated.
The world teaches desire to constantly search for novelty.
Jesus teaches covenant faithfulness.
The world says, “Upgrade.”
Covenant says, “I still choose you.”
The world trains the eyes to wander.
Grace teaches the eyes to come home.
Maybe that is one of the most beautiful things a husband can communicate to the wife who no longer feels beautiful:
“I still see you.”
Maybe that is something a wife can communicate to a husband quietly wondering whether age has made him undesirable:
“I still want you.”
There is nothing inherently unholy about those words.
Within faithful, loving marriage, they can become medicine.
Because sometimes what your spouse desperately needs is not another theological lecture about marriage.
Sometimes they need to know they are still cherished.
Still wanted.
Still beautiful to the person who promised to stay.
Proverbs does not tell the husband merely to endure the wife of his youth.
It tells him to rejoice in her.
To be satisfied in her.
To be captivated by her love.
That is not lust masquerading as marriage.
That is marital delight being directed toward covenant faithfulness.
Hebrews 13:4 says marriage is to be honored and the marriage bed kept undefiled.
Notice the biblical balance.
Marriage bed.
Undefiled.
Intimacy and holiness are not enemies.
The Bible refuses both distortions.
It refuses the culture that says, “If you desire it, do it.”
And it refuses the shame-based distortion that whispers, “If you desire anything sexually, you must be dirty.”
Jesus offers something better.
Desire redeemed by covenant.
Passion governed by love.
Bodies treated with honor.
Sexuality surrendered to Christ.
Faithfulness reaching all the way into the imagination.
And grace for sinners who have failed.
Because perhaps you are reading this and the conversation has suddenly stopped being theoretical.
Maybe your eyes have wandered.
Maybe pornography has trained your mind to consume bodies instead of love people.
Maybe you have mentally compared your spouse to images on a screen.
Maybe you have carried fantasies you would be terrified for your husband or wife to see.
Maybe you have used “marital rights” as an excuse for selfishness.
Maybe you have withheld affection as punishment.
Maybe you have rejected your spouse so repeatedly that they have begun wondering whether something is wrong with them.
Maybe shame has frozen something beautiful between you.
Maybe adultery was not merely in your imagination.
Maybe there was a message.
A conversation.
A secret account.
A hotel room.
A betrayal.
And now this article hurts.
Good.
Not because condemnation is the destination.
Because sometimes pain is what happens when light reaches an infected wound.
Jesus did not expose sin so sinners would have nowhere to go.
Jesus exposed sin and then walked toward the cross.
That is the Gospel.
Christianity is not the announcement that respectable people behaved themselves.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ came for sinners.
For adulterers.
For the sexually broken.
For the ashamed.
For the addicted.
For the betrayed.
For the betrayer who genuinely repents.
For husbands who failed.
For wives who failed.
For people who have memories they wish they could erase.
For people who have spent years hiding behind church clothes while carrying secret chains.
Christ does not call darkness light.
Grace never requires God to lie about our sin.
He names it.
He judges it as sin.
And then at Calvary, the sinless Son of God bears judgment for sinners.
That is why repentance is not running away from Jesus.
Repentance is finally stopping your running from Jesus.
You turn around.
You confess.
You stop defending what is killing you.
You bring the hidden browser history.
The secret fantasy.
The bitterness.
The shame.
The betrayal.
The wounds.
The distorted understanding of sex.
The fear of intimacy.
The years of pretending.
You bring it into the light.
And you discover that the Savior standing there already knew.
He knew before the nails.
And He went to the cross anyway.
This does not make repentance unnecessary.
It makes repentance possible.
This does not make holiness optional.
Grace teaches us to leave sin, not rename it.
But your scandal does not have to write the final sentence of your story.
Jesus can.
From scandal...
to grace.
From secrecy...
to confession.
From objectification...
to honor.
From betrayal...
perhaps, through repentance and patient rebuilding, toward restoration.
From shame...
toward freedom.
From distorted desire...
toward desire surrendered to Christ.
So no—simply enjoying your spouse’s body is not what Scripture means when it condemns lust.
The Bible itself can celebrate marital physical delight.
The better question is not merely, “Do I experience desire?”
Ask:
What is my desire doing to the person I claim to love?
Does it honor covenant?
Does it remain faithful?
Does it recognize my spouse as an image-bearer rather than a possession?
Can it hear “not now” without becoming cruel?
Can it remain tender when bodies change?
Does it seek mutual good rather than selfish consumption?
Does it draw marriage toward faithfulness rather than importing other people into the imagination?
Can this desire stand honestly before Jesus Christ?
Those questions expose the difference between merely baptizing selfish appetite and receiving marital sexuality as something to steward under the lordship of Christ.
And maybe someone reading this has spent years feeling ashamed for loving their own husband or wife.
Hear this carefully.
You do not become holier by becoming ashamed of everything God created good.
You become holy by surrendering everything—including your sexuality—to Jesus Christ.
Desire does not need to become your master.
Neither does shame.
Christ is Lord over both.
You can simply write, “Jesus, purify my heart.”
If your marriage has been wounded but you believe Christ is still working, comment, “Christ is still healing us.”
If shame has followed you into your marriage and you are finally realizing that biblical holiness and marital affection are not enemies, comment, “Grace is teaching me.”
You do not have to publish the details of your private life.
But sometimes three honest words are the first crack in a wall we have spent years building.
Then send this to your spouse.
Send it privately to the believer fighting pornography.
Send it to the couple trying to rebuild after betrayal.
Send it to the Christian who loves Jesus but has never been taught a biblical theology of marital desire.
Save it too.
Because culture will keep preaching about sex.
Shame will keep preaching about sex.
Pornography will keep preaching about sex.
Your past may keep preaching about sex.
You need to remember what Scripture actually says.
It cannot.
It does not.
And certainly not because God needs your money.
He does not.
Scripture says giving must not be “of necessity” or under compulsion, because God loves cheerful giving (2 Corinthians 9:7).
But voluntary financial partnership has long helped Gospel ministry travel farther than one person could carry it alone.
If you genuinely believe this work glorifies Christ, supporting it is one practical way you can participate in helping it continue and expand.
And sharing costs nothing.
You may never know what God does with that simple act.
Bring your desires to Christ.
Bring your marriage to Christ.
Bring your wounds to Christ.
Bring your sexuality to Christ.
Bring your secret failures to Christ.
Bring your shame to Christ.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where Christ is calling you toward forgiveness.
Seek wise pastoral or professional help where wounds run deep.
Rebuild trust where trust has been shattered.
Honor your spouse.
Guard your eyes.
Guard your imagination.
Cherish the covenant God has entrusted to you.
And remember this when shame comes knocking again:
Jesus did not die to make you less human.
He died to redeem the human being sin had broken.
Your body belongs under His lordship.
Your desires belong under His lordship.
Your marriage belongs under His lordship.
And when Jesus becomes Lord even there—in the places Christians sometimes feel too embarrassed to discuss—shame no longer gets to write the ending.
Because the deepest question was never simply whether you desired.
It was whether your desire had learned to love.
And when even the most wounded places of your life are surrendered to Christ, the sentence shame thought was final can become the place where grace begins writing again.
